'''''Oenanthe fistulosa''''', '''tubular water-dropwort''', is a [[flowering plant]] in the [[Apiaceae|carrot family]], native to [[Europe]], [[North Africa]] and western parts of [[Asia]]. It is an uncommon plant of [[wetland]]s, growing around pools and along ditches, mainly in areas of high conservation value.

==Description==
[[File:Oenanthe fistulosa umbel Stodmarsh.jpg|thumb|The outermost flowers in each umbel have enlarged "radiating" petals]]
Tubular water-dropwort is a hairless, [[stolon]]iferous [[perennial]] growing up to 80 cm tall with brittle, hollow, inflated cylindrical stems 0.5 cm in diameter, which are constricted at the nodes (hence the specific name [[Fistula|''fistulosa'']]). Unlike some other water-dropworts, it has no swollen tubers among the roots, but it can reproduce vegetatively by the lengthy stolons.<ref name=Sell3>{{cite book |last1=Sell |first1=Peter |last2=Murrell |first2=Gina |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland, vol 3 |date=2009 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge}}</ref>

The leaves vary widely in shape, with the upper ones being typically [[pinnate]] and having narrow, almost linear segments, while the lower ones can be 2- or even 3-times pinnate, with broader, flat leaflets, more like those of other [[Apiaceae|umbellifers]]. The [[petiole (botany)|leaf stalks]] of the upper leaves are fistular, like the stem, and longer than the pinnate leaf blade.<ref name=Tutin>{{cite book |last1=Tutin |first1=T.G. |title=Umbellifers of the British Isles |date=1980 |publisher=Botanical Society of the British Isles |location=London}}</ref>

It flowers between July and September in northern Europe, with clusters of 2-4 [[umbel]]s about 1 cm in diameter, each of which has numerous white to pinkish flowers. A distinguishing feature is that, unlike many other umbellifers, it has no [[bract]]s but only small bracteoles on the individual umbels. The rays (stalks to the umbels) are 10–30 mm long and become thicker after flowering.<ref name="Tutin" /><ref name="Sell3" />

Plants are monoecious, with [[hermaphrodite|hermaphroditic]] and male flowers on the terminal umbels, and only male flowers on the lateral umbels. Each flower has 5 unequal [[petal]]s with the larger, outer ones radiating, 5 [[stamen]]s and 2 prominent [[Stigma (botany)|styles]] arising from a swollen base (stylopodium) at the top of the ovary. After flowering, the flower stalks and fruits expand to form distinctive pink balls with the remains of the styles projecting in pairs from the surfaces of the cone-shaped fruits.<ref name="Tutin" /><ref name="Sell3" />

==Taxonomy==
The scientific name for tubular water-dropwort was coined by [[Peter Artedi]], who developed the modern [[Binomial nomenclature|binomial]] classification system, and defined the species on the basis of its [[Bract|involucral]] characters.<ref name=constance>{{cite book |last1=Constance |first1=L. |title=History of the classification of Umbelliferae (Apiaceae) ''in Heywood, V. H. (ed.) The Biology and Chemistry of the Umbelliferae''|date=1971 |publisher=Academic Press |location=London |pages=1–11}}</ref> It was published after Artedi's death by [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] in [[Species Plantarum]], in 1753, and that name still stands, although numerous others (synonyms) have been proposed over the years, including ''Phellandrium fistulosum'' (L.) Clairv. (1811), ''O. filipendula'' Dumort. (1827) and ''Selinum fistulosum'' (L.) E.H.L. Krause (1904). A full list can be found in the Synonymic Checklists of the Plants of the World.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hassler |first1=M. |title=Synonymic Checklists of the Vascular Plants of the World |date=2024 |publisher=ChecklistBank |doi=10.48580/dgjc7-3dd |url=https://www.gbif.org/dataset/be1f0e7a-0ee0-45a8-847c-9d12e3997425}}</ref>

A few subspecies and variants have been named, such as forma ''submersa'' (Glück, 1936), subspecies ''fistulosa'' (Linnaeus, 1753) and var. ''tabernaemontani'' ((C.C. Gmel.) DC., 1830), but none is in common use now.

There are no reported hybrids.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=Hybridization and the Flora of the British Isles |date=1975 |publisher=Academic Press |location=London |isbn=0-12-661650-7}}</ref>

Its chromosome number is 2''n'' = 22.<ref name=Tutin/>

The generic name ''[[Oenanthe (plant)|Oenanthe]]'', which comes from the [[Ancient Greek]] οίνος, "wine" and άνθος, "flower", was used in ancient times for certain Mediterranean plants and later adopted to describe this genus. "[[Fistula]]" is the Latin for tube, and refers to the shape of the stem. The "dropwort" part of the common name is a reference to the tubers produced amongst the roots of certain other species in the [[Oenanthe (plant)|genus]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Wiktionary |title=dropwort |date=18 August 2024 |url=https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/dropwort}}</ref>

==Identification==
It can be distinguished from other British species of ''Oenanthe'' by its inflated hollow stems (those of ''lachenalii'' and ''pimpinelloides'' are solid); the absence of bracts (present in ''crocata'', ''lachenalii'' and ''pimpinelloides''); the fruit being globose with all fruits sessile (not so with ''crocata'', ''silaifolia'', ''pimpinelloides'' or ''lachenalii''); and the fruits being less than 4 mm long (more in ''crocata'' and ''fluviatilis'').<ref name=Kent>{{cite web |last1=Kitchener |first1=G.D. |title=Kent Rare Plant Register: Oenanthe fistulosa L. (Tubular Water-dropwort) |url=https://bsbi.org/download/24773/ |access-date=1 May 2022}}</ref>

==Distribution and status==
The global range of tubular water-dropwort is from Europe through the northern half of [[Africa]] to western parts of [[Asia]]. It occurs no further north than southern Scandinavia and is rare as an introduction beyond  its natural range. In [[Great Britain|Britain]] and [[Ireland]] it is found mainly in the lowland eastern counties, becoming increasingly rare towards the uplands of the north and west.<ref name="Tutin" /><ref>{{cite web |last1=Global Biodiversity Information Facility |title=''Oenanthe fistulosa'' L. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/5371890}}</ref> In France the pattern is similar, with the main populations in the southern lowlands, becoming rarer towards the upland regions around the [[Alps]].<ref name=IPNI>{{cite web |last1=Inventaire National du Patrimoine Naturel |title=''Œnanthe fistuleuse'' |url=https://inpn.mnhn.fr/espece/cd_nom/109869/tab/statut}}</ref>

The [[International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] threat status is Least Concern (LC) (as assessed in 2013), both globally and in Europe.<ref>{{cite web |last1=IUCN Red List |title=Tubular Water-dropwort |url=https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/164499/42323299 |access-date=19 December 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=European Environment Agency |title=''Oenanthe fistulosa'' L. |url=https://eunis.eea.europa.eu/species/151660 |access-date=29 April 2022}}</ref> In [[France]], it is similarly considered unthreatened nationally, but in some reasons it is declining, notably in [[Limousin]], where it is Critically Rare (CR), and [[Midi-Pyrénées]], where it is Endangered (EN).<ref name="IPNI" /> It is also declining in some other European countries, such as [[Slovenia]], where it is classed as EN.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kuhar |first1=U. |last2=Kržič |first2=N. |last3=Germ |first3=M. |title=Habitat characteristics of threatened macrophyte species in the watercourses of Slovenia |journal=Internationale Vereinigung für theoretische und angewandte Limnologie: Verhandlungen |date=2009 |volume=30 |issue=5 |pages=754–756 |doi=10.1080/03680770.2009.11902232|s2cid=135206453 }}</ref>

In [[Great Britain|Britain]] it is classified as Vulnerable (VU), while in [[England]] it is believed to have declined by 35% in its area of occupancy between the 1960s and the 1990s. This decrease appears to have continued in some English counties, such as [[Kent]], where the number of sites has shrunk by 60% between the 1970s and 2005, despite it being a Biodiversity Action Plan species.<ref name="Kent" />

==Habitat and ecology==
[[File:Illustration Oenanthe fistulosa0 clean.jpg|thumb|Botanical drawing of tubular water-dropwort]]
It is a wetland plant, occurring naturally in swamps and marshes along valleys and in river deltas such as the [[Camargue]] in France<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Corre |first1=J.J. |title=Etude phytoecologique des milieux littoraux sales en Languedoc et en Camargue II |journal=Vie et Milieu |volume=28 |pages=1–49 |url=https://www.sussex.ac.uk/affiliates/halophytes/index.php?content=plantView&id=91}}</ref> and the [[Doñana National Park]] in Spain.<ref>{{cite book |last1=García-Murillo |first1=Pablo |title=Las plantas de la marisma del Parque Nacional de Doñana (España) |date=2014 |publisher=Universidad de Sevilla |url=http://www.scielo.org.mx/pdf/cuat/v9n1/2007-7858-cuat-9-01-00060.pdf}}</ref> In well-drained agricultural landscapes it is now more likely to be found in drainage ditches, farm ponds and grazed wet meadows. In some places it is found as a [[halophyte]] in coastal dune slacks or brackish grazing marshes, as at [[Aiguamolls de l'Empordà]] in Spain<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Watt |first1=S. |last2=Vilar |first2=L. |title=A comparative study of the vegetation at Aiguamolls de l'Emporda wetlands (N.E. Iberian peninsula) |journal=Scientia Gerundensis |volume=23 |pages=109–154 |url=https://www.raco.cat/index.php/Scientia/article/download/45569/55133}}</ref> or on the [[Sefton Coast]] in Britain.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Smith |first1=Philip H. |title=An inventory of vascular plants identified on the Sefton Coast |date=2005| url=https://www.seftoncoast.org.uk/pdf/smith_200511.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Smith |first1=Philip H. |title=Tubular Water-dropwort on the Sefton Coast sand-dunes, Merseyside |journal=BSBI News |date=2010 |volume=113 |pages=13–19 |url=https://archive.bsbi.org.uk/BSBINews113.pdf}}</ref>

It favours clean, [[Trophic state index|mesotrophic]] water, slightly base-rich conditions, and moderately high light levels, which make it an [[axiophyte]] in most British counties.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Stroh |first1=Peter |title=BSBI species accounts: Oenanthe fistulosa L. |url=https://bsbi.org/wp-content/uploads/dlm_uploads/Oenanthe_fistulosa_species_account.pdf |access-date=31 January 2015}}</ref> In France it is an indicator of the ''[[Gratiola officinalis]]-O. fistulosa'' community in restored wetlands along the [[Saône]] river.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Godreau |first1=V. |last2=Bornette |first2=G. |last3=Frochot |first3=B. |title=Biodiversity in the floodplain of Saone: A global approach |journal=Biodiversity and Conservation |date=1999 |volume=8 |issue=6 |pages=839–864 |doi=10.1023/A:1008807328566 |s2cid=42241272 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/225311160}}</ref> In contrast, it is dominant in a type of flooded [[Agrostis stolonifera|creeping bent]] meadows on clay in Italy, in a ''[[Ranunculus ophioglossifolius]]''-''O. fistulosa'' community.
<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Biondi |first1=E. |last2=Blasi |first2=C. |last3=Allegrezza |first3=M. |title=Plant communities of Italy: The Vegetation Prodrome |journal=Plant Biosystems |date=2014 |volume=148 |issue=4 |pages=728–814 |doi=10.1080/11263504.2014.948527|hdl=11573/732263 |s2cid=86528842 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

In places where it has noticeably declined, attempts have been made to restore its habitat. Wet meadows were sown in the valley of the [[Meuse]] in NE [[France]], but after three years it had not colonised them.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Vécrin |first1=M.P. |last2=Diggelen |first2=R. |last3=Grévilliot |first3=F. |title=Restoration of species-rich flood-plain meadows from abandoned arable fields in NE France |journal=Applied Vegetation Science |date=2002 |volume=5 |issue=2 |pages=263–270|doi=10.1111/j.1654-109X.2002.tb00556.x }}</ref> However, when a species-poor ditch in an area of arable farmland in [[Romney Marsh]] was cleared and planted up, ''O. fistulosa'' thrived for at least a while, showing that it is not as sensitive to nutrient enrichment as some species.<ref name="Kent" />
[[File:Depressaria daucella Marden Meadow.jpg|thumb|Larva of the moth ''Depressaria daucella'' on tubular water-dropwort flowers at Marden, Kent]]

Its [[Indicator value|Ellenberg values]] in Britain are L = 7, F = 9, R = 7, N = 6, and S = 0.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hill|first1=M.O.|last2=Mountford|first2=J.O.|last3=Roy|first3=D.B.|last4=Bunce|first4=R.G.H.|title=Ellenberg's indicator values for British plants. ECOFACT Volume 2. Technical Annex|date=1999|publisher=Institute of Terrestrial Ecology|isbn=1870393481|url=http://nora.nerc.ac.uk/6411/1/ECOFACT2a.pdf|accessdate=29 May 2017}}</ref>

Like other umbellifers, tubular water-dropwort has unspecialised flowers that are pollinated by a wide variety of beetles, flies and other invertebrates. Only a few insects have been found to feed on it: the larvae of the beetle ''[[Lixus paraplecticus]]'' are phytophagous within the stems; [[Papilio machaon|common swallowtail]] caterpillars eat the leaves (in France); and the larvae of the moth ''[[Depressaria daucella]]'' cause mines within the leaves or feed on the foliage and flowers.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Biological Records Centre |title=Insects and their food plants |url=http://dbif.brc.ac.uk/ |access-date=30 April 2022}}</ref>

There are two fungi which cause [[gall]]s in tubular water-dropwort in Britain: ''[[Protomyces macrosporus]]'' causes distortion and swelling of the leaves, petioles and stems, while ''[[Uromyces lineolatus subsp. nearcticus|Uromyces lineolatus]]'' produces yellowish spots on the lower surface of the leaves and petioles.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Redfern |first1=Margaret |last2=Shirley |first2=Peter |title=British Plant Galls |journal=Field Studies |date=2002 |volume=10 |pages=207–531 |isbn=1-85153-214-5}}</ref>

==Uses==
Tubular water-dropwort roots have been found to contain small quantities of [[Oenanthotoxin]], the toxic agent that makes [[Oenanthe crocata|hemlock water-dropwort]] so dangerous. However, the quantities are much (10 x) lower and it is generally considered safe, or even palatable.<ref>{{Cite journal

}}</ref> ''Oenanthe fistulosa'' is freely grazed by livestock. It is used in traditional medicine in Algeria and investigations into the essential oil show there are constituents that could have medical benefits as well as a chemical, [[Heneicosane]], which attracts mosquitoes involved in transmitting [[Dengue fever]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Seenivasagan|first1=T|last2=Sharma|first2=KR|last3=Sekhar|first3=K|last4=Ganesan|first4=K|last5=Prakash|first5=S|last6=Vijayaraghavan|first6=R|title=Electroantennogram, flight orientation, and oviposition responses of Aedes aegypti to the oviposition pheromone n-heneicosane.|journal=Parasitology Research|date=March 2009|volume=104|issue=4|pages=827–33|doi=10.1007/s00436-008-1263-2|pmid=19018567|s2cid=6880282}}</ref>

It has been reported as part of the traditional cuisine in parts of southern [[Italy]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Savo |first1=Valentina |title=When the Local Cuisine Still Incorporates Wild Food Plants: The Unknown Traditions of the Monti Picentini Regional Park (Southern Italy) |journal=Economic Botany |date=2019 |volume=73 |pages=28–46 |doi=10.1007/s12231-018-9432-4 |s2cid=59525209 |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12231-018-9432-4|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and [[Turkey]], where it is known as Gazyak or Kazayağı (a general name for various species of water-dropwort), and the basal leaves are cooked as a meal.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Doğan |first1=A. |last2=Bulut |first2=G. |last3=Tuzlaci |first3=E. |title=A review of edible plants on the Turkish Apiaceae species |journal=Journal of the Faculty of Pharmacy of İstanbul Üniversity |date=2014 |volume=44 |pages=251–262}}</ref>

The Irish botanist D.E. Allen suggests that ''O. fistulosa'' might be the plant that was reported in [[County Wicklow]] as a treatment for [[rheumatism]].<ref name=Allen>{{Cite book |last1=Allen |first1=D.E. |url=https://archive.org/details/medicinalplantsi00davi |title=Medicinal Plants in Folk Tradition |last2=Hatfield |first2=G. |year=2004 |publisher=Timber Press |isbn=0-88192-638-8}}</ref>
